PullRequest.Title: automations: preserve run history and filter editor sessions
PullRequest.Body:

Fixes #339352
Ref: #337757, #343008

## Motivation

Removing an Automation definition or restarting Agent Host should not make its run history disappear or lose the provider that owns it. Automation runs also belong in Automation history, not the ordinary editor Sessions list. This PR persists typed provider and backend provenance, makes recovery and deletion use that identity, and filters Automation runs from editor discovery while preserving explicit history access.

History cleanup must also survive partial deletion, a lost response, provider reconnect, or process restart without blocking unrelated Automation mutations. Retained owners therefore keep only the identity, name, and history metadata needed to manage them later.

<summary>Code stats</summary>

- **Total diff:** +2,995/-193 across 49 files
- **Implementation:** +1,471/-161 across 31 files
- **Tests:** +1,518/-30 across 17 files

- **Split:** 51.2% implementation, 48.5% tests, 0.3% documentation

Largest files:

- `agentHostAutomationService.test.ts`: +497/-7

<details>
<summary>Change breakdown</summary>

| Category | What it does |
|---|---|
| Durable provenance pipeline | Carries central Automation origin through V2 catalog projection, state, listing, restore, and local/remote provider caches |
| Run lifecycle and recovery | Journals creation and exact ownership; keeps minimal retained owners; checkpoints deletion outside the shared mutation queue |
| AHP history choices and consumers | Negotiates keep/delete, durable receipt acknowledgement, later delete/retry, tools, UI, and accessible output |
| Editor filtering | Excludes typed Automation runs from ordinary discovery while retaining direct history access |

- **Durable provenance pipeline:** `agent.ts`, `agentService.ts`, `sessionState.ts`, `persistSessionMetadata.ts`, catalog projection/list/source files, state mirror/manager files, local/remote provider files, `AUTOMATIONS.md`, and their tests.
- **Run lifecycle and recovery:** `agentHostAutomationService.ts` and `agentHostAutomationService.test.ts`.
- **AHP history choices and consumers:** extension protocol/client/server files, Automation metadata helpers, local/null host services, Automation stores and aggregate service, tools, Automations view/accessibility, shared Automation contract, and their tests.
- **Editor filtering:** `agentSessionsModel.ts`, `agentHostSessionListController.ts`, `agentHostSessionListStore.ts`, and their tests.

</details>

## Changes made

- Persist typed Automation origin and exact provider/backend identity before publishing run history, then use it for restart recovery and legacy backfill.
- Keep the catalog at payload V2. Older-writer, canonicalization/hash, pending-write, and new → old → new compatibility tests preserve central `sessionOrigin` without requiring V3.
- Persist cumulative host deletion receipts until the client confirms its cleanup journal, so partial failure and lost responses remain recoverable.
- Run slow backend deletion outside the shared Automation mutation queue while short durable checkpoints serialize state.
- Replace retained executable definitions and customization references with minimal inert owners.
- Expose **Delete Run History** for retained owners and **Retry Delete Run History** after interrupted cleanup, with matching context-menu, accessible-help, and accessible-view state.
- Exclude Automation runs from ordinary editor Sessions discovery while keeping them openable from Automation history.

## Validation

- **Original adjacent suites:** 3,391 passed, 28 pending, 0 failed.
- **CCR adjacent suites:** 929 passed, 1 pending, 0 failed.
- **Post-merge combined suites:** 4,996 passed and 28 pending; the 10 failures are pre-existing comparison-group CSS pixel assertions in an untouched main file (`0.666667px` vs `1px`).
- **Post-merge overlap suites:** 823 passed, 1 pending, 0 failed; the targeted Automation Sessions-list policy test also passed.
- **Final CCR regressions:** 252 passed, 0 failed.
- **Latest-main Automation/wake overlap:** 1,452 passed, 16 pending, 0 failed.
- **Latest-main provider/cleanup overlap:** 1,754 passed, 11 pending, 0 failed.
- **Latest-main protocol overlap:** 850 passed, 1 pending, 0 failed.
- **V2 compatibility matrix:** 11 passed, covering older-writer edits, V2 canonicalization/hash, malformed/hash fallback, pending snapshots, provider restoration, and new → old → new recovery.
- **Focused lifecycle regressions:** durable lost-response receipts, cumulative partial-failure acknowledgement, minimal owners, concurrent request coalescing, non-blocking mutations, retained-history delete/retry, protocol version skew, and accessible availability all passed.
- **Coverage mode:** 2,501 passed, 17 pending, 0 failed; Windows produced a zero-byte `lcov.info`.
- `npm run typecheck-client`, `npm run valid-layers-check`, full-repository ESLint (13,903 files), and `git diff --check` passed.
- `npm run hygiene` remains blocked in this Windows worktree by the existing absolute-path duplication `C:\C:\...\remote\package.json`.
- Controlled restart, provider-unavailable, pending-snapshot, partial-failure, lost-response, and cleanup-resume fixtures passed without mutating external resources.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The changed critical path, nested cardinality, unbounded retained run map, and eager callers are directly visible. Exact milliseconds depend on profile history size, which affects severity rather than mechanism confidence.
Findings.PerformanceResource: synchronous CPU work comparing every persisted Automation run and its session arrays for every listed session
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Each listSessions call now does O(S × R × K) matching work for S registered sessions, R retained Automation runs, and average K sessions per run; ordinary sessions never receive an origin and therefore repeat the full miss scan on every refresh.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: increased startup and Sessions-list refresh latency, with event-loop CPU pressure on profiles containing substantial session and Automation histories
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Catalog-served rows and provider fallbacks were returned after their bulk/session metadata reads; listing did not traverse the Automation run history for each row.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Both catalog-served and fallback rows now call _withAutomationSessionOrigin, which calls getLegacySessionOrigin whenever origin is absent; that helper linearly traverses the unbounded _runs map and checks run.sessions.includes.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added return wrapper at agentService.ts:5251 moves legacy-origin lookup onto every catalog-served session in listSessions; before this diff the same row returned directly without any Automation-run traversal.
Findings.Title: Index legacy origins instead of scanning every run per session
Findings.Impact: Opening VS Code or refreshing Agent Host sessions eagerly calls listSessions. A profile with hundreds or thousands of ordinary sessions and retained Automation runs performs the complete run-history scan once per session before the list response can complete; the four-way async limiter does not parallelize this synchronous scan.
Findings.Evidence: AgentService.listSessions maps every catalog result through the added call at line 5251 (and the analogous fallback call), while _withAutomationSessionOrigin invokes AgentHostAutomationService.getLegacySessionOrigin for every origin-less row. getLegacySessionOrigin loops all _runs and performs run.sessions.includes; _runs retains all terminal history rather than the 50-item presentation window (withRunWindow only slices summaries). BaseAgentHostSessionsProvider eagerly awaits listSessions to initialize its cache, and AgentHostSessionListStore uses the same call for refreshes.
Findings.Recommendation: Build and maintain a session/provider-to-origin index once from _runs and _sessionCreations (updating it on run mutations), or bulk-resolve all missing origins once per listing. Preserve the existing positive backfill write, but make ordinary-session misses O(1) so later refreshes do not rescan history.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The serial call path, full-file flush implementation, and 102-session exercised scenario are explicit. Storage size and provider deletion duration vary by profile, so magnitude is uncertain but the I/O amplification is not.
Findings.PerformanceResource: backend session-deletion calls plus whole Agent Host storage JSON serialization, temporary-file writes, renames, and removals
Findings.PerformanceScaling: For N retained session identities, deletion is strictly serial and performs N backend deletes and at least N full storage-file flushes; legacy entries without a recorded provider add another full flush each. Because every checkpoint serializes all remaining Automation runs and a growing deletedSessions array, bytes serialized/written grow approximately quadratically with N.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: excessive filesystem I/O and long blocking latency for Delete Run History, with lower deletion throughput as history grows
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Removing an Automation performed one catalog/storage mutation and did not place per-history-session backend deletion plus durable full-file rewrites on this request path.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new _deleteHistory loop awaits deleteSession for one entry and then awaits _recordDeletedHistorySession before proceeding; that method calls _persist, whose setAndFlush rewrites the complete Agent Host storage JSON to a temporary file and renames it.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added await at agentHostAutomationService.ts:552 forces a full durable checkpoint after every newly introduced per-session deletion before the loop can advance.
Findings.Title: Checkpoint history deletion in bounded batches
Findings.Impact: Deleting retained history with many runs waits for every backend operation and durable rewrite in sequence. The added test explicitly exercises 51 runs with two sessions each (102 identities), which entails over one hundred whole-file writes before the command returns, and histories are retained beyond the 50-row published page.
Findings.Evidence: agentHostAutomationService.ts:541-552 serializes the per-entry boundary calls. _recordDeletedHistorySession calls _persist after every success; _persist materializes all runs/maps and AgentHostStorageService writes JSON.stringify(this._data) to a temp file, renames it, and removes the temp file. The new 'deletes all retained members beyond the history page' test establishes a realistic effective cardinality of 102 session deletions.
Findings.Recommendation: Keep crash recovery, ordering, and exact receipts, but process a bounded batch of session deletions and persist one compact checkpoint per batch (or move deletion progress to an incremental journal) rather than rewriting the entire Automation store after every member. Use bounded concurrency only if provider disposal semantics permit it.

Scenarios.Scenario: Eager Agent Host session discovery and later Sessions-list refreshes
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The host's listSessions response must finish before the local/remote provider can initialize or refresh its authoritative session cache; every catalog-served and fallback row now passes through legacy Automation-origin resolution.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Bulk-read central session catalog rows, with bounded provider/session-database fallback for ineligible rows
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One central bulk read for S candidates plus fallback reads only for ineligible rows
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same bulk/fallback reads occurred, after which rows were returned directly.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Must complete before the listing response; unchanged batching remains efficient.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist a newly inferred Automation origin into central session state
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most once per positively matched legacy Automation session after persistence; ordinary misses perform no I/O
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No origin backfill write occurred during listing.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Awaited before the matched row can return, though coalesced flush mode reduces write count.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: S registered sessions multiplied by R retained Automation runs and each run's session-membership array; ordinary sessions dominate realistic profiles and remain origin-less, so their misses recur.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Fallback metadata resolution is limited to four promises, but getLegacySessionOrigin is synchronous JavaScript inside each task, so each row's full run-map scan consumes the event loop rather than gaining boundary parallelism.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The central catalog is bulk-read and frontend providers have warm caches, but invalidation still calls listSessions. Positive legacy matches are persisted with coalesced writes; negative ordinary-session misses have no cache/index and rescan all runs on every host listing.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high: the added list wrappers, linear run traversal, unbounded retained run map, and eager callers are directly traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact latency depends on accumulated session/run counts and average sessions per run, but the O(S × R × K) repeated CPU mechanism remains and grows persistently for negative misses.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable high-severity repeated-work regression: every origin-less listed session now scans all retained runs, including on ordinary-session misses that repeat forever.

Scenarios.Scenario: Delete an Automation and all retained run history
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The client journals and flushes its request, sends one IPC request, then waits for the host to delete every member, publish catalog removal, return exact receipts, persist client cleanup, and acknowledge the host receipt before the action resolves.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One delete request and one acknowledgement per durable request ID after client-side coalescing
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Deletion used the existing catalog action path and had no history-choice extension round trip.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Both are awaited by the user action.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Resolve provider registration and dispose each retained backend session through AgentService
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One provider lookup only for identities lacking stored provider, and one session disposal per distinct retained backend session
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Automation removal did not fan out into per-history-session backend disposal on this path.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Each disposal is awaited serially before the next member.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Rewrite and durably flush the complete Agent Host storage JSON after each provider resolution/deleted member and at final completion
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At least N+1 full-file writes for N members; up to roughly 2N+1 when provider identities must first be recorded
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Removal performed a single Automation storage mutation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Every checkpoint is awaited before the loop advances, directly extending deletion latency.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Flush client pending-deletion and acknowledged-cleanup journals
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: A bounded handful of flushes per coalesced delete request, independent of N after backend-session grouping
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No client deletion receipt journal existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required before dispatch and acknowledgement to preserve recovery semantics.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: N distinct backend session identities across all retained runs, including members beyond the 50-row published history page; the added test uses 51 runs and 102 distinct sessions.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Client requests and host requests are coalesced per Automation. Within one host deletion, backend session disposal and durable checkpoints are fully serial; different interrupted Automations can recover concurrently, while short storage mutations serialize through the shared queue.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: There is no cache for deletion. Durable host receipts and client journals make retries coalesce and avoid re-deleting already checkpointed members; warm retry state narrows work to remaining sessions.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high: the per-entry awaited loop, full-store setAndFlush implementation, and 102-member test establish the boundary fan-out and write amplification.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Backend disposal and disk durations vary, but the serial N-call and N-full-write cardinality is fixed by code; large histories are explicitly supported beyond the page limit.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable medium-severity I/O regression: durable progress rewrites the whole storage file after every member instead of checkpointing bounded batches or an incremental journal.

Scenarios.Scenario: Create and start an Automation run with durable provenance
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Allocate an unused identity, persist running state plus creation intent, create the provider session, persist linked membership/origin, then send the initial prompt; these steps intentionally gate execution to prevent replay after restart.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist allocated identity/creation intent and then linked run membership in Agent Host storage
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Two durable Automation-store flushes per newly created run, matching existing run-state/link checkpoints in count while carrying additional identity data
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Running state and session linkage were already persisted around provider creation; the diff adds exact allocated identity to those checkpoints.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Both complete before the initial prompt is sent.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Mint/register the provider session and persist typed SessionOrigin metadata
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One allocation and one session creation per run
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Session creation minted its own identity and did not persist typed Automation origin.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send the initial Automation message to the created provider session
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same initial send followed session linking.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Marks useful execution start and remains after durable linkage.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One session identity for a normal run, with cost independent of total visible session count except that full Automation storage serialization includes retained run state.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Run-state changes serialize through the Automation mutation queue; provider session creation and initial send run outside it. Existing scheduling determines how many pending runs start, with no new aggregate burst proven by this diff.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Provider availability is observed; no cache miss fan-out is introduced. Persisted creation intents are removed after linking and reused only for recovery.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: ordering and boundary count are explicit in the changed run-start path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Storage blob size grows with history, but the diff does not add a new per-item loop or extra checkpoint count for a normal run.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional finding: the placement is an intentional durability tradeoff and no independent new fan-out beyond the existing run lifecycle is established.

Scenarios.Scenario: Agent Host restart recovery for old runs and interrupted history deletion
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Startup loads Automation storage, restores minimal history owners/provider identities, then schedules run recovery, deletion recovery, and normal Automation scheduling. Owner restoration is awaited before scheduling; backend deletion work runs outside the shared mutation queue.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Resolve registered provider for legacy run sessions
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Until one provider is found per legacy run lacking runProviders; normally zero for already-migrated/warm state
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Startup did not restore missing retained owners or backfill their provider identity.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Owner restoration awaits these lookups before Automation scheduling begins.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist migrated owners/providers once after restoration
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One full Automation-store flush if catalog/provider state changed

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Delete remaining backend sessions for interrupted deletions
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One disposal per remaining checkpointed member; no repeats for successfully checkpointed members
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runs asynchronously after startup owner restoration and does not hold the shared mutation queue across slow deletion.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Legacy runs missing provider provenance, number of sessions per such run, and number of interrupted deletion resources/members.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Provider restoration is sequential during startup. Interrupted deletions are coalesced per Automation and can run concurrently across Automations, with one backend deletion at a time per Automation and serialized durable checkpoints.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Recovered provider identities are persisted, so the migration lookup is primarily cold/one-time. Completed member checkpoints and receipts survive restart; warm retries process only remaining members.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: cold versus warm migration behavior and per-resource coalescing are directly implemented and tested.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The prevalence of old runs lacking provider provenance and simultaneous interrupted deletions is unknown; expected warm-state cost is small.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate finding: cold migration is persisted, deletion retries are coalesced, and slow backend cleanup is deliberately kept off unrelated mutation critical paths. The per-member flush issue is already reported in the deletion scenario.

Scenarios.Scenario: Render Automation history and filter Automation runs from the ordinary Sessions list
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Automation view updates synchronously derive visible runs/history owners and update bounded DOM rows; ordinary Sessions discovery materializes/deduplicates its in-memory collection and filters typed Automation metadata before rendering.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Published Automation history rows (50 per page unless explicitly paged), retained owners, provider count, and ordinary session count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Synchronous UI/model work only; no subprocess, IPC, filesystem, database, or network boundary is reached from the changed render/filter code.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: ProviderAutomationService and reconnectable stores cache runsFor observables by Automation ID and invalidate them on deletion. Typed origin is retained in provider caches, avoiding the old run-history-to-session marker recomputation.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: changed UI paths only query in-memory observable/store state and manipulate existing bounded history rows.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Users can page more history, but no forced layout, eager hidden heavy component, or unbounded retained DOM mechanism was found.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding: added work is bounded in-memory projection/DOM state, while typed origin removes the previous catalog-based session-marker recomputation.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 49 changed files. Reported two diff-introduced regressions: quadratic legacy-origin lookup on every session listing and per-session whole-file checkpointing during retained-history deletion. Reviewed startup recovery, run creation, protocol/journal boundaries, provider caches, UI rendering, and editor filtering; no other high-confidence performance issue or qualifying regression-fix record was established.
